metadata.rules_text:
- When sentiment is consistently negative (last 3–5 days) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast by 5–15% to avoid overconfidence in recovery.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior peak), model tends to overshoot — cap forecast at 1–2 days above peak or use 3-day moving average to smooth.
- If sentiment is positive but price is trending down, model often fails to recognize mean reversion — adjust forecast downward by 3–8% for 3–5 day horizon.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral, model overfits recent volatility — use 10-day rolling average or ignore last 2–3 days of history for forecasting.
- If true outcome is significantly below forecast (e.g., >15% under), check if sentiment was positive — if so, reduce forecast by 10–20% for next 3–5 days.
- If true outcome is significantly above forecast (e.g., >15% over), check if sentiment was negative — if so, increase forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates downward trends — add 2–5% buffer for negative sentiment or 1–3% for positive sentiment.
- If sentiment is positive and price is falling, model may misread sentiment — use sentiment as a multiplier (e.g., 0.8–0.9 if sentiment >0.3) to dampen forecast.
- If sentiment is negative and price is rising, model may overreact — reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.
- Always check if forecast is trending upward from a recent low — if so, model may be overestimating — reduce by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.
